theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go. All prices and exchange rates in this test are made up for the questions.

essays.stem: Describe the purchasing cycle for the steel and consumables on a fabrication job, from the first request to paying the supplier and reviewing its performance. Say who does each step and what record is kept.
essays.modelAnswer: The supervisor or estimator works out what is needed from the drawings and raises a requisition, which is approved by the manager. The buyer, with the supervisor, writes a full specification: grade, sizes, finish, certificates and delivery date. The buyer sends a request for quotation to approved suppliers, then compares the quotes on price, quality, delivery and service, and records the comparison. After any fair negotiation, the buyer raises a numbered purchase order, which is approved within the spending limits. The buyer expedites the order before the due date. When the goods arrive, the storekeeper checks them against the order and certificates and records the receipt. Accounts match the invoice with the order and the receipt before paying, within the agreed terms. Finally, the buyer records the supplier's performance, such as on-time delivery and rejects, and uses it when choosing suppliers next time. All records are filed with the job.
markingPoints: Requisition raised and approved from the job's needs
Full specification and RFQ to approved suppliers
Quotes compared, order raised and approved within limits
Expediting, receiving and checking against order and certificates
Invoice matched and paid; supplier performance recorded

essays.stem: Explain how you would set up and use a weighted scoring sheet to choose a supplier for the structural steel on a job. Include a short worked example.
essays.modelAnswer: First I decide what matters for this job, such as price, quality (correct grade, certificates, few rejects), delivery (on time, can meet the date) and service (cutting, advice, after-sales). I give each a weight that adds to 100%, for example price 50%, quality 30% and delivery 20%. I agree the weights with the manager before the quotes come in, so the choice is fair. Each supplier is scored out of 10 for each item, using its quote and past records. I multiply each score by its weight and add them. For example, Supplier X scores 8 for price, 6 for quality and 9 for delivery: 8 × 0.5 + 6 × 0.3 + 9 × 0.2 = 4 + 1.8 + 1.8 = 7.6. Supplier Y scores 9, 5 and 6: 4.5 + 1.5 + 1.2 = 7.2. X wins, even though Y is cheaper. I record the sheet and the reasons with the order, so the decision can be checked later.
markingPoints: Chooses sensible criteria for the job
Sets weights adding to 100%, agreed before quotes arrive
Scores suppliers and multiplies by the weights
Works a correct example
Records the sheet and reasons with the order

essays.stem: Explain what makes up the landed cost of stainless steel sheet imported into Jamaica, and the steps and documents needed to bring it in.
essays.modelAnswer: The landed cost is everything paid to get the sheet to the workshop. It starts with the supplier's price, which may be in US$, so I convert it at the exchange rate on the day, allowing for the rate moving before payment. If the price is FOB, I add sea freight and insurance; if it is CIF, these are included to Kingston port. Then I add customs duty and other import charges, and GCT at the current rate, the customs broker's fee, port charges, and haulage from the port to the workshop. Only with all of these can the imported sheet be compared with sheet bought locally. The steps are: place the order with a clear specification, arrange or confirm shipping, and get the commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading and mill certificates. The broker clears the goods through customs. The sheet is collected, delivered and checked against the order and certificates when it arrives.
markingPoints: Defines landed cost as the full cost to the workshop
Converts US$ and allows for exchange rate risk
Explains FOB versus CIF and adds freight and insurance
Adds duty, GCT, broker, port and haulage costs
Lists the documents and the clearing and checking steps

essays.stem: Explain what a purchase specification for steel plate and welding consumables on a coded job must include, and why each part matters.
essays.modelAnswer: For plate, the specification gives the grade and the standard it is made to, so the strength and weldability are right. It gives the thickness, width and length and the number of pieces, so the right sizes arrive and waste is low. It asks for mill certificates with the actual test results for each heat, so the steel can be traced and the inspector can accept it. It may ask for a surface condition, such as free from heavy rust or laminations, and for marking with heat numbers. For consumables, it gives the exact electrode or wire class named on the WPS, the diameter, the pack size and the batch certificates, because a different class could make the procedure invalid. It states packaging, such as sealed tins for low-hydrogen electrodes, so moisture is kept out. For both, it gives the delivery date and address, the quantity, and who to contact, so the goods arrive when and where needed.
markingPoints: Grade and standard, with the reason
Sizes and quantities, with the reason
Mill certificates with actual results and heat marking for traceability
Exact consumable class, size and batch certificates, matching the WPS
Packaging, delivery date, place and contact

essays.stem: Compare one-off orders, blanket orders with call-offs, and consignment stock as ways of buying welding consumables, and say when you would use each.
essays.modelAnswer: A one-off order buys a set quantity for one job, with its own quote and order. It suits special items, such as a stainless wire or a special flux needed only for one job. It takes more paperwork if used for everyday items. A blanket order agrees prices and terms with one supplier for a period, such as a year, and the shop calls off quantities as it needs them. It suits items used every week, such as grinding discs, E7018 electrodes, MIG wire and gas, because prices are fixed, ordering is quick and stock can be kept low. Consignment stock is kept in the shop's store but still belongs to the supplier until it is taken out and used, then it is paid for. It saves the shop's cash and keeps items on hand, but needs careful counting and an agreement on who is responsible for damage. I would use consignment for high-use wire and electrodes if a supplier offers it.
markingPoints: Explains one-off orders and when they suit
Explains blanket orders and call-offs
Gives the benefits of blanket orders for regular items
Explains consignment stock and who owns it
Gives sensible uses and a drawback of consignment

essays.stem: Explain how a fabrication shop decides whether to make parts itself or buy them in, such as laser-cut plates or galvanising, and what a purchase order for a service must state.
essays.modelAnswer: The shop compares the full cost of making the part with the cost of buying it. Making it includes material, labour, machine time, consumables and the cost of mistakes; buying includes the price, delivery and the time to check it. The shop also thinks about quality and accuracy, whether it has the equipment and skills, how busy its own staff are, and how quickly the part is needed. For example, 40 identical plates with holes may be cheaper and more accurate from a laser cutter, while galvanising must be bought in because the shop has no bath. A purchase order for a service must describe the work exactly: the items and quantities, the drawings, the standard or finish required, such as the coating to be applied, any tests or inspection and certificates, the delivery date and transport, and the price and payment terms. It should also give special warnings, such as sealed hollow sections that need vent holes.
markingPoints: Compares the full cost of making with the full cost of buying
Considers quality, equipment, skills, workload and time
Gives a sensible example of each choice
Service order states items, drawings, standard or finish and checks
States delivery, price, terms and special warnings

essays.stem: The Centre is a public body. Explain how its purchasing of materials must be open and fair, and what a buyer must and must not do when running a tender.
essays.modelAnswer: The Centre spends public money, so the procurement rules for public bodies require it to buy openly, fairly and for good value, and to be able to show this later. For a large purchase, the buyer runs a tender. The buyer must write a clear specification that does not favour one firm, send the same information and closing date to all bidders, and answer any questions to all of them at once. Bids are kept sealed and secure until the closing time, then opened with a witness and recorded. They are judged only on the criteria and weights stated in the tender. The buyer must declare any link to a bidder, such as a relative, and step back from the decision. The buyer must not share one bidder's price with another, accept gifts, split orders to avoid the rules, or let a late bid in. Every step is recorded, so an auditor can check that the process was fair.
markingPoints: Explains why: public money, fairness and value
Clear, neutral specification and the same information to all
Sealed bids, opened with a witness, judged on stated criteria
Declares conflicts of interest
Lists things a buyer must not do, and keeps records for audit

essays.stem: Explain how you would plan the purchase of four new welding machines for the Centre's workshop, from deciding what is needed to accepting them.
essays.modelAnswer: First I agree what the machines must do: the processes, such as MMAW, GMAW and FCAW, the current range and duty cycle needed for training, and that they suit the Centre's supply, for example 220 V, 50 Hz single-phase, as checked by the Centre's electrician. I write a specification without naming a brand. I ask approved suppliers for quotes and compare the whole cost of owning each machine over its life, not just the price: guns, consumables, servicing, spare parts held in Jamaica, warranty, and the training the supplier gives. I check what other users say about service. After approval and a purchase order, I plan the delivery and installation with the electrician. When the machines arrive, I check them against the order, make sure the manuals and warranty papers are there, have them installed and tested, and only then sign for them. I add them to the equipment register with their serial numbers and service dates.
markingPoints: Defines needs: processes, range, duty cycle and supply
Neutral specification and quotes from approved suppliers
Compares whole-life cost, spares, service and warranty
Plans delivery and installation with the electrician
Checks, tests and records the machines before accepting

essays.stem: Explain how you would monitor a supplier's performance, and what you would do about a steel supplier whose deliveries are often late or wrong.
essays.modelAnswer: I keep records for each supplier: orders placed, the date each was promised and delivered, items rejected or short, wrong certificates, and how quickly problems were put right. From these I work out simple measures, such as the percentage of deliveries on time and the reject rate, and review them every few months. If a steel supplier is often late or wrong, I first gather the facts from the records. I meet the supplier, show the figures, and ask for the causes and a plan to fix them, with dates. I may agree changes, such as earlier order dates, clearer specifications on our side, or a check before loading. I record what is agreed and keep watching the figures. Meanwhile, I make sure an approved second supplier can be used for urgent work. If there is no improvement, I report to the manager and the supplier may be removed from the approved list.
markingPoints: Keeps delivery, reject and problem records
Works out measures such as on-time rate and reject rate
Meets the supplier with facts and agrees a plan
Keeps a second supplier ready and records agreements
Reports and removes the supplier if there is no improvement

essays.stem: Explain how a minimum and maximum stock level and the economic order quantity (EOQ) help a buyer plan purchases of high-use consumables, and the limits of these methods.
essays.modelAnswer: A minimum stock level is the point at which a new order is placed, set so that the stock will not run out while waiting for delivery. A maximum level is the most that should be held, so cash and space are not wasted. When stock falls to the minimum, the buyer orders enough to bring it back to the maximum. The EOQ uses a formula with the yearly usage, the cost of placing each order and the cost of holding one item for a year, to find the order size that keeps the total of ordering and holding costs lowest. For example, discs used at 1 200 a year, J$1 500 per order and J$40 to hold each disc gives an EOQ of 300. These methods help the buyer avoid both shortages and overstock. But they assume steady use and steady prices. They do not handle sudden big jobs, price breaks, shelf life, or supply problems such as hurricanes, so the buyer must still use judgement.
markingPoints: Explains the minimum level and why it is set
Explains the maximum level and ordering up to it
Explains EOQ and what it balances
Gives a correct example
Gives at least two limits of the methods

practical1.title: Request quotations, compare suppliers with a weighted scoring sheet and raise a recommended purchase order for a fabrication job (role play)
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a job pack: a materials list for a fabrication job (such as steel stair stringers and treads, with the welding consumables and gas), the Centre's approval limits, and information sheets for three made-up suppliers with prices, delivery times, terms and past performance. Each member takes a named role and produces part of the evidence: the buyer writes the full specification and the request for quotation (RFQ); two members play supplier representatives who answer the RFQ with written quotes from their sheets; the evaluator builds the weighted scoring sheet, with weights agreed with the group before the quotes are opened, and works out the total cost of each quote (including delivery and GCT at the current rate, as the assessor gives it); and the approver plays the manager. The buyer holds a short, fair negotiation with the best two suppliers and records the outcome. The group then writes a one-page recommendation and a numbered purchase order, which the approver checks against the approval limits. Photograph each stage below.
materials: Job pack with materials list and the Centre's approval limits (from the assessor)
Information sheets for three made-up suppliers (from the assessor)
Blank RFQ, quotation, scoring sheet, recommendation and purchase order forms
Calculators, or a computer with a spreadsheet
Flip chart or whiteboard and markers
photos: The written quotes from the two supplier role players
The weighted scoring sheet with totals worked out
The negotiation role play in progress, with the notes
The recommendation and the approved purchase order
checklist: Played the named role fully and produced his or her part of the evidence
The specification gives grade, sizes, quantities, certificates and delivery
Weights were agreed before the quotes were opened and add up to 100%
Total costs and weighted scores are worked out correctly
The negotiation was fair, honest and recorded
The purchase order is complete, numbered and within the approval limits
safety: Use only the made-up suppliers in the pack; no real firm's names or prices
Keep each supplier's quote confidential within the role play
Speak respectfully in the negotiation; no pressure or false claims
Share the workload fairly so every member takes part

practical2.title: Plan and cost an import purchase of stainless steel sheet and fittings, and present the purchasing plan to the manager
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group a pack for a job that needs stainless steel sheet and fittings that must be imported: the quantities and specification, a made-up overseas quotation in US$ (on FOB or CIF terms), freight and insurance figures, an exchange rate, duty and fee figures, local haulage cost and the date the materials are needed on the job. Each member takes a named part: one works out the landed cost in J$ on the costing sheet (with GCT at the current rate, as the assessor gives it); one draws a timeline (bar chart) from order to delivery, working back from the job date, with lead time, shipping, clearing and a margin for delays; one makes a checklist of the documents needed (purchase order, commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading, mill certificates) and who supplies each; one lists the risks (exchange rate, late shipping, hurricane season, wrong grade) with a control for each; and one compares the landed cost with a local supplier's price from the pack. The group then presents its plan to the assessor, who plays the manager and asks questions. Photograph each stage below.
materials: Import job pack with all figures (from the assessor)
Blank costing sheet, timeline grid, document checklist and risk table
Calculators, or a computer with a spreadsheet
Flip chart or poster paper and markers
photos: The timeline from order to delivery
The group presenting the plan to the manager
checklist: Produced his or her named part of the plan
The landed cost includes every charge and is worked out correctly in J$
The timeline works back from the job date and allows for delays
The document checklist is complete and says who supplies each document
The risks are real and each has a sensible control
Answered the manager's questions clearly during the presentation
safety: Use only the made-up figures and firms in the pack
Keep prices and the Centre's budget figures confidential
Treat each other with respect during the presentation and questions
Share the workload fairly and keep to the time allowed
